speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Chairman, I beg to move, "That the total sum to be allocated for Head N of the Estimates be reduced by $100." I still recall vividly the images of the fall of the Berlin wall as a child.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This was the physical manifestation of the "iron curtain" and its fall marked the end of the Cold War.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Historians of the time, like Francis Fukoyama described this as the "End of History", the end of mankind's ideological struggle and the triumph of Western liberal democracy.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The subsequent period in the 1990s saw a de facto unipolar world with the former Soviet Union in crisis and the United States (US) as the sole superpower.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Singapore had always been a historic and strong ally of the US in this region, and this marked the way for development of a different kind.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The whole world could come together and look for mutually beneficial economic collaborations.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Economic growth through multilateralism prospered during this period.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This also paved the way for Singapore to engage China more deeply and China-Singapore relations started officially in 1990.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: And this was at a time when many other developed countries had imposed sanctions on China following the Tiananmen Square incident in 1989.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Singapore has always tried to play a constructive role in its international relationships, and I understand that from the start of international relations in 1990, has been a quiet spokesperson championing China's integration into the world economy.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Deng Xiaoping and his team continued economic liberalisation through the 1990s and China grew steadily.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Given China's base of more than a billion people, the effect of economic growth has been phenomenal.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Along with its economic growth, Chinese influence around the world has also grown steadily.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: China has become a major trading partner for most countries, including the US, and a big investor in many regional countries, including in many parts of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN).

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Most of this influence has been positive and mutually beneficial for all countries involved.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: However, there will always be an element of displacement when a new power rises.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: And unfortunately, relations between China and US have taken a more adversarial tone.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The US has accused China of trading "unfairly" and has imposed tariffs on Chinese imports.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This is worrying because it runs counter to all the hard work that has been achieved over the decades since the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade, and subsequently the World Trade Organization (WTO) removed trade barriers and facilitated world trade.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Current trade tensions between the US and China are worrying.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: These tensions are also spilling out into other areas, such as technology.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Singapore has had strong relations with both the US and China.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I would be grateful if the Ministry can also share how Singapore manages relations with both countries and how we can better position ourselves amidst these tensions.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Another manifestation of this tension is in the South China Sea, where China has had competing claims with a number of ASEAN allies and has taken an increasingly assertive stance.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The US, of course, like many other maritime countries with an interest in these straits, has asserted its right of free passage over these waters.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Of course, Singapore hopes the dispute will be resolved in accordance with international law, but that requires all parties involved to willingly submit the matter for determination in the event of a dispute.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: There have been news reports of China's military activities in the South China Sea, while the US and its allies have conducted Freedom of Navigation Operations in the region.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: ASEAN is negotiating a Code of Conduct in the South China Sea with China.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I would be grateful if MFA can provide an update on these negotiations, as well as the outlook for the situation in the South China Sea.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: Chairman, ASEAN was originally an alliance in 1967 between a small number of non-Communist Southeast Asian countries, namely, Singapore, Thailand, Philippines, Indonesia and Malaysia.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: These countries were also our closest neighbours in terms of proximity.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: The relationship was close as we had alignment of interests in economic growth and political and security interests as well.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: Brunei, another close ally and neighbour, became a member in 1984.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: At this time, much of the rest of ASEAN included Communist countries and the Cold War divided us.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: Following the end of the Cold War, ASEAN engaged many of these countries in Indo-China as well as Myanmar, with a view to building mutually beneficial economic relationships.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: Eventually, these countries joined the fold in the course of the 1990s.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: Of course, as any group gets bigger, there are more likely to be differences of opinion and interests, and ASEAN has not been immune to this either.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: In recent years, ASEAN members have had differences over matters, such as the South China Sea and on how to deal with the Rakhine state in Myanmar.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: However, despite these differences, we still have much in common and many areas on which we cooperate.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: Singapore undertook the ASEAN Chairmanship in 2018 when ASEAN was at an inflection point.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: Singapore had sought to foster consensus within ASEAN on some of the key values that should underpin any framework for continued regional engagement.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: This includes ASEAN Centrality, inclusiveness, economic benefits, and support for a rules-based international order.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: Against the backdrop of a retreat from multilateralism and intensifying Sino-US competition which I spoke about earlier, how can ASEAN strengthen its centrality and try to speak in one collective voice on the more contentious regional developments and global issues?

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: Our closest neighbour and with whom we have the strongest ties in terms of culture, relationships and history is Malaysia.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: Singaporeans and Malaysians still make regular trips and the Causeway is the most heavily used link in the world between two countries.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: Most of us still have close family and friends living there.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: As such, it is always sad when relationships between the two governments worsen.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: Following the change of government in Malaysia, there has been an emergence of new tensions in bilateral relations with Malaysia.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: This started with a stalling on joint projects, such as the High-speed Rail and, later, the Rapid Transit System.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: There were also public statements that Malaysia will be reconsidering matters, such as the agreement on water.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: These vessels still remain in our waters although the governments on both sides have taken steps to de-escalate matters.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: Given that Malaysia is our closest neighbour and both countries are highly interdependent, how will Singapore approach its relations with Malaysia going forward such that our national interests are protected and the bilateral tensions do not spill over to negatively impact the lives of our people?

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim (Nee Soon)
text: Mr Chairman, the Pakatan Harapan coalition took over the Malaysian government following the 14th General Elections in May last year.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim (Nee Soon)
text: On the dispute over the extension of Johor Bahru Port Limits, can the Ministry of Foreign Affairs (MFA) provide an update on the working group discussions and whether there has been any progress in terms of resolving the dispute?

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim (Nee Soon)
text: I would be grateful for an update on the discussions on these two issues?

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: Chairman, Indonesia has been a long-standing and close ally of Singapore for many decades and both have been founding members of ASEAN since 1967.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: Next to Malaysia, Indonesia is probably the next closest in terms of culture and proximity.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: Prime Minister Lee and President Jokowi have had a number of high-level meetings, most recently at the Singapore-Indonesia Leader’s Retreat in 2018.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: Would MFA be able to update members of the public on the state of our bilateral relations with Indonesia, including key takeaways from our engagements last year?

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: How will we work to maintain our relationship with Indonesia for the benefit of our peoples?

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: Indonesia's presidential election will be held in April this year.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: How will we continue to engage the next administration and strengthen our bilateral and regional cooperation with Indonesia?

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Mr Chairman, we observe a trend of more countries all over the world, including those in our region, becoming increasingly nationalistic and inward-looking.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The recent elections and change in government in Malaysia had coincided with the emergence of prickly issues in Singapore-Malaysia relations.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: As our other close neighbour, Indonesia, will have its own national elections in April.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: What is MFA's view on the possible impact this could have on bilateral relations with Singapore?

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: What are some of the issues which have been unresolved and could become potential points of contention?

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Which are the main areas of common interests which we can pursue to strengthen our relationship?

speaker: The Chairman
text: Ms Joan Pereira, you can take the three cuts together.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The United Nations (UN) Development Programme, for example, gave us invaluable advice on the formulation of Singapore’s economic development strategy, without which Singapore would not be the success we are today.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The SCP's focus on human resource development reflects our belief that a country's most valuable asset is our human capital.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: World Bank Group president Jim Yong Kim said that "policies that build human capital are some of the smartest investments that countries can make to boost long-term inclusive economic growth." How has SCP, with its focus on developing human capital, helped Singapore to build our international network and standing?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Would the Minister share examples and details of programmes and the impact of these on the relationships between Singapore and the foreign countries involved?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Were there any subsequent projects of mutual collaboration and how have these been beneficial to both Singapore and the partner countries?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The increasing number of trips to destinations further afield, such as Iceland, South America and Africa, in addition to perennial attractions such as Japan, South Korea and Europe, shows how strong our collective wanderlust is.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Given the increasing uncertainty around the world, Singaporeans who travel often or have family and close friends living abroad, would naturally be concerned whenever there is another natural disaster or terrorist attack in the news.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Last year, there were a few major natural disasters, political riots and traffic accidents overseas where Singaporeans found themselves caught in.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: If caught in a major crisis or emergency abroad, our citizens located all around the globe would require more assistance and support from the Government.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I would, therefore, like to know what measures are being taken by MFA to address the needs and expectations of our travelling citizens.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: What travel advice should Singaporeans take note of, especially those who travel to places where consular support is not so accessible?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Lastly, what is the role of our missions overseas in strengthening ties with Singaporeans living or working there?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Our people’s confidence and support are crucial to the success of Singapore's foreign policy, especially in the proliferation of misinformation and disinformation in this digital age.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Technology which allows information to reach us almost instantaneously can also deliver distorted and even false information.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Disinformation campaigns by countries big and small are a relatively low cost means to undermine the will and resolve of other nations that they have disagreements with.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We are one of the most Internet-connected countries, and one of the most diverse nations on earth.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Countries that have differing constituencies and demographic compositions are particularly susceptible to such influence, which can set up contention against one another.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: MFA requires the strong support of a united citizenry to carry out its work effectively.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: It is thus very important for us to ensure that Singaporeans understand the fundamental principles of our foreign policy so that they are able to exercise good judgement and not take in information at face value.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I understand that MFA is expanding its foreign policy outreach to the Singapore public, especially the younger generation and students, to help them better understand Singapore’s foreign policy.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Would MFA please provide an update on these outreach efforts?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Relations among the big powers – the US and China, the US and Russia, are under stress.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: There is an increasing trust deficit among states, and countries are questioning the benefits of multilateralism, openness, globalisation and free trade.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This has resulted in a growing wave of support for protectionist and isolationist policies in some countries, undermining support for a multilateral, rules-based international order.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We cannot change the fact that Singapore remains a "Little Red Dot" on the map.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We also cannot change our destiny that however the global landscape evolves and whatever challenges we may face, we will always do so as a small state.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Small states like Singapore thrive in a rule-based and rule of law-based international order.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: What can we do to protect and advance our interests in the face of rising unilateralism across the world?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Singapore is nonetheless not alone in being small.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Countries which identify themselves as "small states" make up the majority of the membership at the UN.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: How is Singapore working with other small states in the international community to ensure that our collective interests are secured and that small states continue to be heard?

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Charles Chong, take the two cuts together.

speaker: Mr Charles Chong (Punggol East)
text: Mr Chairman, the relationship between the People's Republic of China (PRC) and the US has been described by a former US Secretary of State as the most important bilateral relationship in the world this century.

speaker: Mr Charles Chong (Punggol East)
text: There is a long and historic relationship with the first voyage of direct trade between the US and China having been recorded as taking place in 1784, some 35 years before Raffles landed in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Charles Chong (Punggol East)
text: So, on the occasion of 40 years of diplomatic relationship between the US and the PRC, I would be grateful if the Minister could provide some insights into how Singapore is affected by the relationship between these two powers, and how we can act in the best interest of Singapore and Singaporeans in navigating our own bilateral relationship between the US and China.

speaker: Mr Charles Chong (Punggol East)
text: The current US administration has been in power for just over two years now.

speaker: Mr Charles Chong (Punggol East)
text: These tensions over the past year have had a negative impact on the global economy and market sentiments.

speaker: Mr Charles Chong (Punggol East)
text: The US and China have imposed tit-for-tat trade tirades on each other, a move which is at odds with Singapore's approach to free and open trade, and one which runs contrary to our support of a rule-based multilateral trading system.

speaker: Mr Charles Chong (Punggol East)
text: Being a small country, we need certainty in terms of how we conduct our trade relations and we value an adherence to well-established international norms, international law and binding contracts between states.

speaker: Mr Charles Chong (Punggol East)
text: So, without repeating the old chestnut involving fighting elephants and grass, I hope the Minister can provide some insights into whether US-China relations have affected the US engagement of Singapore and vice-versa.

speaker: Mr Charles Chong (Punggol East)
text: And if a trade war were to take place between US and China, could the Minister shed some light on how Singapore has prepared ourselves for the follow-up to this?

speaker: Mr Charles Chong (Punggol East)
text: Mr Chairman, the second issue I would like to speak on involves US engagement of Southeast Asia.

speaker: Mr Charles Chong (Punggol East)
text: Singapore has been a long-standing and steadfast advocate of the US engagement of and presence in Asia.

speaker: Mr Charles Chong (Punggol East)
text: We are a key security partner of the US in the region, with our defence relationship being formalised in 2005 through the Strategic Framework Agreement and, subsequently, enhanced in 2015 with the US-Singapore Cooperation Agreement.

speaker: Mr Charles Chong (Punggol East)
text: Since 2002, Singapore has hosted the annual Shangri-la Dialogue where Asia Pacific countries, including the US and Southeast Asia Nations come together to discuss defence and security issues, thereby contributing to the enhancement of defence diplomacy amongst participating countries.

speaker: Mr Charles Chong (Punggol East)
text: But it is not just defence and security matters where there will be at a strong relationship.

speaker: Mr Charles Chong (Punggol East)
text: Indeed, the US and Singapore have a strong partnership in many other areas.

speaker: Mr Charles Chong (Punggol East)
text: These days, however, the US appears to be focused on other regional matters, such as the denuclearisation negotiations in North Korea.

speaker: Mr Charles Chong (Punggol East)
text: And what does it mean for the US commitment to the region as well as its initiatives to engage Singapore and the rest of Southeast Asia?

speaker: The Chairman
text: Ms Tin Pei Ling, you can take the two cuts together.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: China and the US are in the midst of a protracted trade war.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: These two countries are the world's two largest economies.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: The Clash of the Titans has disrupted the global economy, with rounds of negotiation, deadlines, headlines and all.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Institutions like WTO are coming under attack, and politicians in many countries are unfortunately attributing the cause of their countries’ domestic problems to free trade.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: There is a surge in protectionism and anti-globalisation in much of the developed world.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Should multilateralism decline or fail, we risk being at the mercy of bigger countries.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: In this challenging environment, what can Singapore do to uphold the open rules-based multilateral trading system?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: And as multilateralism come under threat, we should look to other emerging markets for new opportunities.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: As a country whose lifeblood is trade and connectivity, Singapore should always be on the lookout for opportunities to build new economic ties and strengthen existing ones.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: The economic potential of Central and Eastern Europe should not remain untapped.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Over the last year, we deepened our relationships with several Central and Eastern European countries.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Given these conditions, how is Singapore continuing to engage the emerging economies in Central and Eastern Europe?

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Loh Thia Khiang, you can take both your cuts.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: Chairman, Sir, as a highly connected small city-state at the heart of Southeast Asia, Singapore is extremely vulnerable to upheavals in the region.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: China’s peaceful economic rise has taken a different turn with military manoeuvres in the South China Sea and its soft and hard power diplomacy vis-a-vis individual ASEAN states.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: China’s rise has led other powers to turn to Southeast Asia.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: America was the first to do a pivot to Southeast Asia, entering into bilateral comprehensive partnerships with ASEAN member states.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: India elevated its “Look East” policy to the "Act East" policy in the shadow of China's One Belt One Road investments in South Asia.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: Japan has also shifted its geostrategic focus from Asia Pacific to Indo-Pacific.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: We have forged close relationships with the US and then with rising China, and more recently India, guided by economic pragmatism and geopolitical realism.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: We have maintained our sovereignty and our commitment to peace and international rule of law.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: We should continue to do all these, but does the new complex environment mean that Singapore should consider pursuing its own strategic pivot to Southeast Asia?

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: There are at least two reasons why we should focus on Southeast Asia.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: First, ASEAN is fast becoming an economic powerhouse.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: ASEAN has a young population, many countries are still in the earlier phases of development, so there is a lot of scope for growth.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: We should not miss this new growth story, right here in our neighbourhood.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: Second, with the global and regional powers turning their strategic focus to Southeast Asia, we should be careful.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: History has shown that when the great powers turn to a region and bring their strategic interests to bear on the countries, well-meaning intentions could easily turn to hostile rivalries.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: We cannot afford to let the powers compete over us and disrupt our unity with divide-and-rule or containment strategies.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: We have been painstakingly building up ASEAN after the Cold War.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: In the event that great power conflicts should erupt again, Singapore would fare better in an ASEAN standing strong together against foreign interference.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: Realising the ASEAN motto of "One Vision, One Identity, One Community" may well be the key to Singapore's survival and success for the next 50 years.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: The American political scientist who pioneered the concept of soft power, called the ability to combine hard and soft power in a successful strategy, "smart power".

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: It is time we deepen our soft power diplomacy to effectively implement what I believe should be a strategic shift to focus our foreign policy on Southeast Asia.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: Since 2015, communications consultancy Portland and the University of Southern California have published Soft Power 30 Index to measure the soft power of the top 30 countries on the international stage.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: It comes with no surprise that the report ranked Singapore top in the category of "enterprise" due to our favourable business, rule-of-law and innovation environment.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: The "smart nation" initiative, underpinned by excellent digital infrastructure and digital government, has also led to a high ranking in the category of "digital".

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: We need to change the perception of our neighbours of Singapore as an arrogant nation that likes to compare itself favourably to other developing countries.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: Oftentimes, the perceived condescension is due precisely to our success as a business hub and a global city adopting the most advanced technologies.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: Success breeds envy among neighbours, and this envy can turn toxic if our neighbours come to believe that our success is due to our taking advantage of their weaknesses.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: I believe we can do three things to enhance our soft power diplomacy to correct the perceived condescension and prevent envy from turning toxic on us.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: First, our government-to-government engagement should deepen with the objective of facilitating economic development of our neighbouring countries.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: We have done so much with China in this respect.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: Is there a reason why we are not reaching the same level of intense engagement with our ASEAN neighbours?

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: Second, ASEAN is made up of countries with complex histories and cultures.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: We are one ourselves, and it will take more than government-to-government engagements to develop our soft power diplomacy.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: We should enhance our people-to-people networking at institutional and practitioner levels for our cultural sector.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: We have signed arts and culture agreements with Australia and China that had led to intense professional exchanges and curatorial collaboration between museums.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: We should do the same with our ASEAN neighbours, especially since we share much historical and cultural kinship.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: Third, we should turn our attention to digital diplomacy.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: We already have the digital infrastructure to do so.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: The next step is to develop our capabilities in making use of it to achieve our diplomatic objectives.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Our Strategic Framework Agreement with the US, for example, formalises bilateral security and defence cooperation.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: We have both also enjoyed many years of exchanges, including high level ones.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: It is also Singapore's largest source of foreign direct investments (FDIs).

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Conversely, Singapore is the US' second largest Asian investor, after Japan.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Besides our regular defence collaboration and exchanges, we are also very active in the US-led Global Coalition to Defeat the Islamic State of Iraq and Syria (ISIS) and we are the only Asian country to have contributed both in terms of military assets and personnel towards this.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: With the new developments in the US, internally and also in terms of its global status, how will Singapore continue to strengthen and deepen our cooperation and relationship with the US?

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Mr Henry Kwek, you can take both cuts please.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Chairman, our bilateral relations with China are excellent, and has been described as "progressive, forward-looking and strategic".

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: In the joint statement issued during PRC Premier Li Keqiang's official visit to Singapore last November, both sides also reaffirmed the principles of mutual respect, sovereign equality and non-interference in each other's internal affairs.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: At the same time, both sides also continued with frequent high-level exchanges and enjoy good cooperation in diverse fields.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: We will celebrate the 25th anniversary of the China-Singapore Suzhou Industrial Park this year.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: We celebrated the 10th anniversary of the Sino-Singapore Tianjin Eco-City Project last year.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: During the same visit by Premier Li, both sides signed several memorandums of understanding (MOUs) covering areas ranging from trade, finance, cooperation on the Belt and Road Initiative (BRI), culture and the environment, among others.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Foreign Minister provide an update on the state of our relations with China?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: How is the progress of our government-to-government relations?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: The choice of Singapore as the venue of the Summit reaffirmed our reputation as an impartial, reliable and safe country.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: The Joint Statement signed by the US and DPRK in Singapore is an important first step forward.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Both sides have since kept up dialogues and exchanges.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Many Singaporeans, including myself, welcome the positive developments on the Korean Peninsula and hope that the dialogue and efforts towards lasting peace and prosperity on the Peninsula will continue.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Could MFA provide its assessment of the developments on the Korean Peninsula, and what role is Singapore playing to support diplomatic efforts towards a peaceful and de-nuclearised Korean Peninsula?

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Mr Chairman, our Leaders, including the Prime Minister, Emeritus Senior Minister and Mr Lee Kuan Yew have had frequent meetings with their Chinese counterparts and enjoy good relations with them.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Deputy Prime Minister Teo Chee Hean has also been described by former Chinese Vice Premier, Mr Zhang Gaoli, as an old and good friend.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Notably, in conjunction with the 40th anniversary of his reform and opening up, China post humorously conferred our Mr Lee Kuan Yew the Reform and Friendship Award in December 2018, in recognition of Singapore and Mr Lee's long-standing support for China's reform and opening over the years.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Our good relations with China did not happen by chance.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: It was cemented by cooperating on a wide span of areas from economic cooperation, sustainable development, human resource development to social governance.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: It is also heartening to see that our 4th Generation (4G) leaders are aiming to maintain the momentum of cross-partnerships by taking the lead in many engagements with China.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Many of our younger Ministers are leading the engagements via the Bilateral Trade Councils established with the Chinese provinces.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: For instance, Minister Heng Swee Keat is the Singapore Chairman for the Jiangsu Bilateral Trade Council and Minister Chan Chun Sing is the Singapore Chairman for the Chongqing Connectivity Initiative.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: As our economic ties deepened, more young Singaporeans will find opportunities to study and work in China.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Ultimately, cooperation between two countries is based on each dealing with its internal challenges and opportunities and working with each other to advance common interests.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: How do we intend to take this mutually beneficial cooperation between Singapore and China to the next level?

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: We had established trade and investment links with the major economies and have a wide network of bilateral and multilateral FTAs.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: These are all part of the soft infrastructure needed to support Singapore companies’ reach overseas to tap new opportunities and markets abroad.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu
text: There are many emerging economies with vast markets and youthful populations.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Mr Chairman, as small countries and, more importantly, as neighbours , Singapore and Brunei shared many similarities and a strategic outlook on many regional and international issues.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: It is this that has led to a special relationship between our two countries, one that has been built over many years and on a foundation of deep, personal and institutional ties dating back to the close relationships shared from the 1960s by the late Seri Begawan and Minister Mentor Lee Kuan Yew.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Having had the honour to visit Brunei on a number of occasions as part of official delegations, including that of then President Dr Tony Tan's State visit in 2013, I must attest that the genuine warmth and welcome that our Bruneians extend to us is extraordinary.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: It is also noteworthy that President Halimah Yacob chose Brunei as a destination of her first State Visit in May 2018 and we have a steady stream of high-level mutual visits every year, including the Annual Singapore-Brunei Young Leaders Programme.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In her toast speech at the State banquet hosted by Sultan Hassanal Bolkiah for her State visit, President Halimah emphasised that future generations of leaders on both sides have the responsibility to build on the existing relations between Singapore and Brunei and to bring those ties to greater heights.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: It is, perhaps, also opportune for us to congratulate our Bruneian friends on the occasion of their 35th National Day this day and may our relations continue to grow ever stronger.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: (In Mandarin):   Arts and culture can become Singapore's soft power to open windows of the world.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: With the support from the Government, enterprises and various funds, the Singapore arts and culture brand has formed its unique style in the international arena.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: Arts and culture play a very important role in diplomacy among countries.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: Going forward, I hope more local arts groups can be invited to perform overseas through strategic MOUs signed between our Government and other countries.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: I hope this kind of performances can be sustained, so that it can improve the standard of our arts and cultural groups which may one day match that of top overseas arts groups.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: (In English): In today’s uncertain geopolitical landscape, where aggressive and hard strategies may do more harm than good, soft power is key for small countries like Singapore, where it is even more important to rely on our positive attraction and persuasion to increase relevance to the international community, gaining support for our agenda.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: Soft power is a critical foreign policy tool, and I think we can do more to leverage our soft power, especially through arts and culture.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: Singapore is a harmonious society with a rich and diverse multicultural heritage.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: Establishing Singapore as a cultural presence in the region can add another dimension to our bilateral accounts.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: On this note, I would like to highlight that our arts and culture groups have been flying our flag overseas proud and high!

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: This is in line with the National Arts Council's SG Arts Plan, where we aspire to position Singapore globally, where arts and culture icons and works are appreciated by audiences at home and abroad.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: Our rich cultural heritage and history should also be actively profiled.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: Through arts, cultural diplomacy, Singapore can project global influence and enhance relations with our foreign partners.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: Singapore’s rich and diverse multicultural heritage is one of the defining traits of our country and of our identity as Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: It can also help foster unity, pride and cohesion among our people as it reminds us of our links to society, as well as to the region and the world.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: Cultural diplomacy, which profiles these similarities, as well as our uniqueness, can help to broaden and deepen our bilateral relations with other countries at the people-to-people level.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: It makes for deeper and more direct relationships with our friends in the region.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: This helps to strengthen our networks with our foreign partners, and Singapore's position as a valuable collaborative partner in the region.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: Mr Chairman, we are, after all, a small country and must allocate our resources well, yet also have an effective network with our overseas missions.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: They can play an instrumental role in expanding Singapore’s cultural soft power to increase our presence and space.

speaker: Mr Terence Ho Wee San (Nominated Member)
text: Could the Minister please provide us with an update on what are we doing on this front?

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: Mr Chairman, Sir, over the last 50 years, ASEAN has worked hard to maintain peace and stability in the region.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: ASEAN has succeeded, for most of the part, in achieving this primary directive.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: As of today, the success of ASEAN has allowed it to not only be an enabler of peace, but also an enabler of economic interdependence.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: It is imperative that ASEAN fosters greater economic, social and political collaboration among its constituent nations.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: In regard to economic collaboration, ASEAN should encourage more business exchanges and partnerships in the region.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: These partnerships aim to support the internationalisation of European small and medium enterprises (SMEs) from 23 different countries by placing them across 150 cluster organisations.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: These cluster organisations subsequently penetrate foreign markets in different fields ranging from construction to aerospace vehicles.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: As of last year, they have launched the second generation of the ESCP-4i.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: The ESCP-4i is poised to “support more than 17,000 European SMEs in accessing global value chains and taking a leading position globally”.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: E-commerce presents opportunities not just for consumers, but also for businesses in ASEAN.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: We should utilise the platform of the ASEAN Smart Cities Network to allow for the global expansion of our firms through digitisation.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Mr Chairman, Sir, ASEAN-EU dialogue relations, connecting a combined population of more than a billion people, span more than 40 years.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The relations have led to the identification of common goals and objectives in the areas of political and security cooperation, economic cooperation and sociocultural cooperation.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Much progress has been made on these fronts.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: For the corresponding period, EU exported €91 billion to ASEAN.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The EU is also the biggest provider of FDIs in ASEAN.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: EU and ASEAN have also agreed to resuming talks for a region-to-region FTA.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: On the security front, ASEAN and EU agreed to work together to enhance crisis response and disaster management.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Without a doubt, EU is an important partner of ASEAN.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Singapore took over as country coordinator for ASEAN-EU dialogue relations in August 2018.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It will hold this appointment until August 2021.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In January 2019, Singapore co-chaired the 22nd ASEAN-EU Ministerial Meeting in January 2019 where an agreement in principle was reached to upgrade ASEAN-EU relations to a strategic partnership.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In addition, the ministers from EU and ASEAN discussed cooperation as well as challenges on regional and international issues.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Does Singapore anticipate any issues affecting ASEAN-EU dialogue relations arising from Brexit?

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Mr Chairman, the Rohingya crisis is a full-blown humanitarian crisis with regional consequences.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Voluntary repatriation is not seen as a viable solution by many given that the root cause of citizenship that results in the discrimination and abuse, as well as guaranteed safety, of the returnees, has yet to be resolved.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: The crisis is a sobering reminder that domestic issues can quickly become transnational ones overnight.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Can I please ask the Minister to provide insights on the following: (a) Is the passive non-interference policy of ASEAN still relevant in today’s globalised context?

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: (b) Will ASEAN develop a refugee and asylum policy that includes guidance for action to be taken when a member state’s internal issues cause people to flee to neighbouring states?

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: (c) Will the ASEAN Intergovernmental Commission on Human Rights be further strengthened for conflicts to be escalated to?

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: (d) And will there be a Human Rights Court set up to interpret and enforce the ASEAN Human Rights Declaration?

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Louis Ng, you can take the two cuts together.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I will always remember what I saw, the painful stories I heard and the people, especially the children, I met.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: To be honest, the image of the child with a bullet wound in her arm is still very much in my mind.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My biggest fear now is that these people will be forgotten.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Over a million of them now live in the refugee camps in Bangladesh.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The attention on this issue is diluting as people move on to more recent crises and funding gets diverted away.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But as the Minister stated, "As long as the refugees remain in the camps, and have no jobs and means of livelihood, they will have no future prospects".

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I also agree with the Minister that "we cannot expect quick fixes".

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But we need to remember that in 1991, 28 years ago, 250,000 had already fled to Bangladesh from Myanmar.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This is not a crisis that began last year or a few years ago.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I do understand that this is an issue that we cannot solve on our own.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister and MFA share what plans MFA has in 2019 to support both Myanmar and Bangladesh in finding a long-term solution?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: There is only us, one human family, connected in ways we sometimes forget.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: He stated that he does not foresee that contingency occurring, at least not in the foreseeable future.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It is worrying that they have only managed to raise 2% of this amount so far, as one million refugees need this for their survival.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I appreciate that Singapore is one of the countries that make voluntary contributions to UNHCR annually.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I am glad that in 2016, as a responsible global citizen, we have increased our contributions to UNHCR from US$50,000 to US$60,000.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: On top of this general donation, can we also consider donating to the UNHCR programme for Rohingya refugees specifically?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Our contribution is comparable to those made by other ASEAN countries, but I sincerely hope we can contribute more to help the Rohingya refugees who so desperately need our help.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: Mr Chairman, Singapore is a small and open country and economy.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: It is important for us to maintain strong linkages with all our Southeast Asian neighbours and have strong and reliable partners in the region.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: Singaporeans are also living and working abroad in these countries in greater numbers.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: Some years ago, I was part of an official delegation led by then-Speaker Halimah Yacob to Laos.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: We met Singaporeans who were working and living there.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: I was surprised to meet one who has been living there for more than 20 years.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: There is a young population and a growing middle class.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: There are many work and career opportunities for Singaporeans to contribute towards and learn from.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: Given the growth trajectory and potential of Southeast Asia, there is space to expand our trade, investment and business links with these countries.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: We are more familiar with our immediate neighbours, Indonesia and Malaysia, with whom we enjoy close and long-standing partnerships.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: Beyond them, could MFA provide an update on what Singapore is doing to enhance our political and economic engagement of fellow ASEAN countries, in particular, Thailand, Vietnam, Myanmar, Cambodia, the Philippines and Laos?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In June 2018, India's Prime Minister Modi visited Singapore and was the first Indian Prime Minister to deliver the Shangri-La Dialogue keynote address in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: He acknowledged that the political relations between India and Singapore are among the warmest and closest.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In the same year, in 2018, he made another visit to Singapore in November to speak at the Singapore FinTech Festival.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: During the event, he launched a global platform to connect FinTech firms and financial institutions, beginning with ASEAN and Indian banks, and FinTech companies.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Prime Minister Modi noted that India and Singapore are also working to connect Indian and ASEAN's SMEs anchored on an Indian platform and expanding it globally.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: These are encouraging developments which we should continue to pursue, particularly given that India is one of the fastest-growing economies in the world and a bright spot for our Singapore companies to invest in.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Could MFA provide an update on the Singapore-India relationship?

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: The Middle East appears to be far removed from Singapore, but its complex dynamics reach us across thousands of miles.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: The Israel-Palestine conflict remains of concern to Muslim majority countries and populations.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: There continues to be clashes along the Israel-Gaza border.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Singapore, being in a region dominated by Muslims, requires us to be vigilant regarding these developments.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Singapore is a speck of sand in the politics of the Middle East, but we have old friends there.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: In 1965, Egypt was the first Arab country to recognise Singapore's Independence.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: We also share common interests, such as the need to promote religious harmony.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: There are Singaporean students studying in universities in the Middle East.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Notwithstanding the security challenges in the Middle East, countries in the region present opportunities for our businesses, given their vast markets and youthful populations.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: There is certainly room for us to create closer ties between the South East and the Middle East.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Increasingly, we find that we may have some role in economic diplomacy.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Previous visits by our top leaders have sought to increase business links between our two regions.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: There are many Singaporean companies in the region, such as Keppel and Sembcorp Group.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Recently, Environment and Water Resources Minister and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs Mr Masagos Zulkifli has suggested that Singapore and the Middle East could work together to develop water management technologies.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Given these developments, I would like to ask the Minister to provide an update on our key engagements with the Middle East for 2019.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: How does Singapore balance our engagements with Middle Eastern countries amidst tensions in the region?

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin (Sembawang)
text: Singapore and Japan enjoy a long-standing and close relationship underpinned by multifaceted cooperation, including trade and connectivity, and science and technology.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin (Sembawang)
text: Singapore and Japan also share strong people-to-people relations and cooperate on capacity-building in other countries.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin (Sembawang)
text: There is much that Singapore can learn from Japan's experience in various areas.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin (Sembawang)
text: This being the case, there is room for both sides to build on our existing good bilateral relationship to share ideas and solutions that will help tackle issues of common interest.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin (Sembawang)
text: Some common challenges include ageing and declining populations.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin (Sembawang)
text: Could MFA provide an update on Singapore-Japan relations, in particular, on new areas of cooperation with Japan?

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Mr Chairman, Singapore and the Republic of Korea (ROK) enjoy a close relationship.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We have good economic cooperation and share strong people-to-people ties.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Many Singaporeans have taken an interest in various aspects of Korean culture, such as K-pop, K-drama and K-food.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Last year, we hosted several high-level visits to Singapore, including an introductory visit by the Foreign Minister Kang Kyung-wha in March, followed by a State visit by President Moon Jae-in in July.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: During his visit, President Moon delivered his 42nd Singapore Lecture.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: He said that cooperation between Singapore and ROK would intensify to jointly prepare for the Fourth Industrial Revolution.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: ROK has one of the most innovative economies globally, with a heavy emphasis on smart technologies and focus on research and development (R&D).

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Given Singapore's interest in developing a Smart Nation, there is room for both sides to broaden existing areas of cooperation and tackle common challenges.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Could MFA provide an update on Singapore's relations with ROK, in particular, the areas of our bilateral cooperation?

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: There will also be better intellectual protection for companies and individuals.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Overall, it a pretty optimistic outlook where Singapore and the EU have further opportunities in the many years ahead to strengthen our trade and investment relations as the companies have now improved access to each other’s markets.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Mr Chairman, this year will also be a critical year for the EU because its key institutions will see leadership changes.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: In May, the European Parliament will have its elections, while the European Council and the European Commission will have new Presidents.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: As the overall political climate in Europe is likely to shift, can the Minister provide an update on how we are engaging the EU and its member states in the face of these changes?

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: This is a positive development that will serve to enhance the already robust trade and investment relations with the EU and the individual EU member states.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: Apart from the EUSFTA, what are the other areas in which we can step up our relations with the key partners in Europe?

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: On the same note, with the Brexit deadline fast approaching, Brexit negotiations between the United Kingdom (UK) and the EU are still uncertain.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: Singapore has signed a number of bilateral trade agreements with the EU as a block.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: If Brexit does, indeed, happen, can MFA elucidate: one, how will it potentially affect our relations with both the UK and the EU?

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: How do we plan to manage our relationship with the UK in the post-Brexit era?

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: And two, will there be plans to ink separate agreements with the UK once Brexit is finalised?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Mr Chairman, Canada's interactions with the region, including Singapore, were widely perceived to be underwhelming, largely due to the geographical distance.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: More recently, Prime Minister of Canada Justin Trudeau visited Singapore to attend the 33rd ASEAN Summit and related Summits as the Guest of the ASEAN Chair and demonstrated Canada’s interest in the region.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: It was also a pleasant surprise to learn of Prime Minister Trudeau’s ancestral ties to Singapore.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: While Singapore and Canada may be geographically distant, I believe we do share some key commonalities.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Both countries support a rules-based multilateral trading system and uphold the shared values of multiculturalism.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Prime Minister Trudeau has said that the relations between Singapore and Canada "will only deepen as the CPTPP comes into force and creates new opportunities and good middle-class jobs for people in both our countries".

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Can MFA elaborate on our engagement of Canada, as well as on the emerging areas of bilateral cooperation?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We are, after all, more than 10,000 kilometres (km) away.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Yet, whether it is melting ice caps and rising sea levels, or the possibility of a new trade route, distant Arctic developments affect our very shores.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Can MFA explain how our observership in the Arctic Council contributes to our understanding of how developments in the Arctic impact Singapore?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Can MFA update the House on Singapore’s response to rising sea levels and the possible opening up of the Northern Sea route?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: How should our businesses prepare themselves for the changes in the Arctic?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We are global citizens after all and must seek to help where practicable.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We are a small country with no natural resources, but have successfully harnessed technology, including sensors and automated meters, to fulfil our ambitions of becoming a smart city.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Can we use Singapore’s home-grown innovations and leverage our smart-city experiences to contribute to the "Smart Arctic" within our networks?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The Arctic, with its unique nature and fragile ecosystems, is an important indicator of the planet's health.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Can our academia also contribute to the body of research to inform global intervention?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: That we are 10,000 km away from the Arctic should not stop us from doing our part in the tropics.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: It is a connected world after all, and we can help to drive sustainable practices through regional forums, such as ASEAN.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Going ahead, how can we facilitate more regional understanding of the Arctic concerns?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: How can we continue to meaningfully engage with the Arctic Council and the Arctic Council member states?

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Mr Chairman, turmoil has engulfed the global trading system.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Policies favouring trade liberalisation and economic integration are in dispute.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Some of Singapore's key trading partners have voted for Governments and policies that are hostile to international trade and economic integration.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Big countries are increasingly saying that to trade with them, it is "their way or the highway".

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: These developments are a grave threat to a small country like Singapore, where trade is our lifeblood.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Chairman, the people worldwide who are voting against trade and integration are not doing so out of hatred or xenophobia.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Americans and Europeans are doing so because they feel their jobs and ways of life are threatened by globalisation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Their heartlanders want to know how trade benefits them.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Singapore is a staunch supporter of the open, rules-based multilateral trading system.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: How has Singapore addressed this growing backlash against trade and economic integration around the world?

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: What can we do to uphold the open and rules-based multilateral trading system for the benefit of all?

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: Mr Chairman, after campaigning on a rhetoric of anti-globalisation, the US President Donald Trump had announced his decision to withdraw the US from the Trans-Pacific Partnership (TPP).

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: One of most important strategic objectives of TPP for Singapore was that it would have entrenched the US engagement in the region.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: Without the US' participation in CPTPP, what are the benefits for Singapore to stay in CPTPP?

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: We are confronted with several geopolitical security concerns today.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: In the age of the digital revolution that we live in today, fake news and cybersecurity breaches are increasingly prevalent and have the potential to erode the trust between the Government and society that has been carefully built up over the years.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: Sometimes, these have even become a tool of foreign policy.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: Reports suggest that a range of state and non-state actors are engaging in disinformation operations here, and these operators have used online news articles and social media platforms to influence Singaporeans and legitimise other states' international actions.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: How does MFA intend to combat fake news and educate our citizens properly about our foreign policy, in particular, our younger generation?

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Mr Chairman, in July last year, Dr Henry Kissinger – probably the most senior Secretary of State and Foreign Secretary in the world – declared, "We are in a very, very grave period." We are, in fact, witnessing the rapid unravelling of the post-World War Two global order.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: And this unravelling is being accompanied by profound shifts in the balance of geopolitical power and also by unprecedented leaps in technology.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: And these changes are not a passing transient phenomenon.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: No one knows how long it will take for the world to set onto a new stable trajectory again.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: For Singapore, our external environment, therefore, will be increasingly volatile, ambiguous, complex and uncertain.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: And we cannot afford the luxury of navel-gazing.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: First, Mr Vikram Nair and Mr Charles Chong asked about Sino-US tensions.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: I agree with both Members that this is the most important bilateral relationship in the global system.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: And the ability, or lack thereof, of the US and China to find a new modus vivendi will shape our era.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: The US actually envisioned and underwrote the post-World War Two global order, now 70 years old: "Pax Americana".

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Therefore, it is a completely legitimate political question for American voters to question whether it is worth their while to continue to sacrifice American "blood and treasure" for international interests.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: And there is an increasing bipartisan consensus that America has been taken advantage of by China and must now play hardball.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: On the other hand, China is pursuing the "China dream" and is determined that the "century of humiliation" will not be repeated.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: And countries, including us, will come under intense pressure to choose sides.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Even if current Sino-US trade tensions are resolved, the strategic contest will continue to be waged but it will include areas, such as defence, energy, cybersecurity and even outer space.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: And we can expect this major power rivalry to sharpen, especially in the technological arena.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: The ongoing arguments about 5G technology are a case in point.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Both the US and China know that the first country to master the Fourth Industrial Revolution will have a huge advantage.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Second, the digital revolution has already triggered disruptions in many other parts of the world.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: A rise in computing power, an explosion in big data, as well as progress in automation, robotics, new computational techniques and smart technology, have transformed societies and economies, and disrupted phenomena all over the world, including in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: The digital revolution, which is still in its early phases, has also ushered in a new Gilded Age, where the fruits of economic growth are unevenly distributed.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: The winners in this era are the giant technology companies and the digital oligarchs who control all the data flows.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: The losers are entire industries and less-skilled workers who are at risk of being displaced by these smart technologies.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: They feel squeezed and, especially in the West, there has been a stagnation in middle-class wages for several decades.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Consequently, with the erosion of the middle-class in developed countries, you will see that they are channelling their frustration towards easy scapegoats – the obvious ones – immigration, free trade and, increasingly, you will see that voters in the middle have become disenchanted with mainstream political parties.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Populist politicians, who promise to impose protectionist and nationalistic policies and appeal to primordial loyalties of race, language and religion, are on the rise everywhere.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: We, in Singapore, must not allow these disruptive forces to fracture our own society.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: We can, and we must, master the technologies of the future so that our people, our citizens, can remain successful and united.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Then, and only then, can we preserve our independence and make decisions based on our own sovereign interests.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: The advances in information technology have made Singaporeans far more media-savvy and has exposed us to the crowded marketplace of competing viewpoints and disinformation.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: But we must also be aware that this also raises the risk of us being influenced by foreign entities who are using these new tools, including using them in the political arena.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Third, another worrying consequence of this uneven distribution of growth, both within countries and across countries, is the inevitable rise of protectionism and nationalism across the world.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Around the globe, the right and left political wings have drifted further apart, hollowing out the political centre.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: The far right has responded to popular disenchantment by focusing on immigration and free trade.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: The liberals have tacked even further left and demanded radical redistribution.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: We are not so bad in this House.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: But you can hear faint echoes of those same political siren calls.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: This tumult of domestic politics and political polarisation has created a geopolitical order dominated by increasingly short-term transactional ethos and a zero-sum mindset.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Ms Tin Pei Ling, Assoc Prof Walter Theseira asked about how we will try to uphold the multilateral trading system.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: The free, open rules-based multilateral system actually has underpinned the success of Singapore and ASEAN and has been the formula for peace and prosperity for many decades.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Unfortunately, countries under domestic political pressure increasingly view multilateral agreements on issues, such as trade, climate change, security, arms control, cybersecurity, as shackles on sovereignty and a burden on economic growth.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Therefore, leaders in these countries are resorting to unilateral actions and prefer bilateral instead of multilateral deals.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: They repudiate multilateral approaches and the multilateral institutions that have kept the peace and facilitated prosperity.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: So, over time, trade connectivity may shrink, tit-for-tat action on disputes will increase, and our ability to respond to global challenges like radicalism, cybersecurity and climate change will be impaired.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Left unchecked, this will be a negative-sum game for everyone.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Closer to home, we must remain vigilant about threats to regional stability and security.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: We are witnessing a surge in identity politics and exclusive extremism that raises the risk for radicalism and terrorism in our region.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: The return of ISIS fighters to Southeast Asia and the episodes of violence which we have seen in the southern Philippines last year, are stark reminders that this is a clear and present danger.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Mr Louis Ng also asked about the refugee situation at the Myanmar-Bangladesh border.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: I can tell you this remains an issue of concern.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Senior Minister of State Mohamad Maliki will elaborate on our response later.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: In just the last few days, we have witnessed recent escalations of tension between India and Pakistan – again, another reminder that the old fault lines remain volatile and are susceptible to political exploitation.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Therefore, the question which all Members have posed is: how should we in Singapore respond to these challenges in this current state of the world?

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: I would submit that our foreign policy principles remain as salient today as they were at our Independence when constructed by Mr Lee Kuan Yew and Mr S Rajaratnam.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: First, we must continue to promote a rules-based international order.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: A system that upholds the rights and sovereignty of all states and the rule of law is important, especially to a small city-state like us.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Without it, small countries will have very little chance of survival.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Under a rules-based system, bigger powers do not get a free pass to act as they will.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: But in exchange for that, what they would benefit from is an orderly, stable global environment.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: We all know that in Singapore, our trade volume is three times our GDP.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: I think all Members will agree with me that we must stand up for the multilateral rules-based global trading system.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: This is our lifeblood for us in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
